enrichment.short_title: Neighbour boundary dispute at Further Granary Cottages
key_facts: Neighbours disputed the eastern boundary of No 6 Further Granary Cottages at Wood Dalling, Norfolk.
The missing 1990 conveyance from Sudemoor Ltd meant the registered title plan and property register were the best evidence of what was conveyed.
A 1998 order had fixed the northern boundary but not the full eastern boundary.
At trial the judge preferred evidence about a 1994 wall and witnesses' opinions rather than construing the conveyance against physical features on the ground in 1990.
The Court of Appeal held the eastern boundary was a straight line between point X (western face of the northern pillar of the 1994 wall) and point Y (where posts and chain met the 1988 wall).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from a boundary declaration made by HHJ Barham after a separate earlier trial on water rights.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the judge's declaration set aside and the boundary declared to be a straight line from point X to point Y.
enrichment.ratio: In a registered-title boundary dispute where the filed plan is subject to the general boundaries rule, the court must construe the conveyance by reference to physical features existing on the ground at the date of the original transfer; witness opinions and a landowner's later conduct are irrelevant if the conveyance, properly construed, fixes the boundary elsewhere.
legal_issues: Proper construction of the conveyance and registered title plan
Effect of the general boundaries rule in rule 278
Whether posts and chain in August 1990 delineated the eastern boundary
Interaction between the 1998 northern-boundary order and the eastern boundary

confidence.notes: Detailed boundary reasoning with clear outcome; judges field in source metadata was empty.

enrichment.short_title: Hague Convention return of Belgian children from England

statutes_considered.title: Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction

key_facts: A Belgian father sought return of three children unlawfully removed by their mother from Walcourt, Belgium, to England in March 2002.
Habitual residence in Belgium and the father's rights of custody were not in dispute.
At first instance Singer J accepted an Article 13(b) grave-risk defence based on alleged domestic violence and ineffective Belgian protection.
The Court of Appeal considered the Belgian authorities had been involved with the family and that return was to the jurisdiction, not necessarily to the father alone.
The appeal was allowed and the case remitted to a High Court judge to arrange supervised return to Belgium.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Father's appeal to the Court of Appeal against a first-instance refusal to order return under the Hague Convention.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; case remitted to the Family Division to put return arrangements in place.
enrichment.ratio: Article 13(b) is a high and exceptional threshold; an English court should not treat Belgian child-protection agencies as unable to protect children on return, and return under the Convention is to the state of habitual residence rather than necessarily to the same household situation.
legal_issues: Application of Article 13(b) grave risk of harm or intolerable situation
Discretion whether to order return even if Article 13(b) is engaged
Role of Belgian social services and child-protection agencies
Whether first-instance findings on domestic violence were open on untested affidavit evidence
linked_authorities: Re C (Abduction: Grave Risk of Physical or Psychological Harm) [1999] 2 FLR 478
Re C (Abduction: Grave Risk of Psychological Harm) [1999] 1 FLR 1145

confidence.notes: Full appellate reasoning on Hague Convention law with clear procedural outcome.

enrichment.short_title: Director disqualification for Lloyd's broker grossing up
key_facts: The Secretary of State sought a disqualification order against Jonathan Chapman, managing director of Lloyd's broker J A Chapman & Co Ltd (Chapco).
Chapco had grossed up marine insurance premiums without assureds' informed consent, diverting over US$1.2 million including to offshore Liberian companies.
Chapman had already accepted Lloyd's disciplinary findings and been excluded from Lloyd's membership with a £100,000 fine.
Mr Justice Peter Smith found Chapman's conduct made him unfit to manage a company and rejected procedural objections based on issue estoppel and parallel proceedings.
A nine-year disqualification order was made under section 8 CDDA 1986.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Secretary of State application for a director disqualification order following a section 447 Companies Act inspectors' report.
enrichment.outcome: Disqualification order for nine years; all charges proved.
enrichment.ratio: Knowingly causing a Lloyd's broker to gross up premiums without client consent is dishonest conduct rendering a director unfit to be concerned in company management; section 8 CDDA proceedings are not barred by earlier Lloyd's disciplinary action or a prior civil judgment where the defendant did not contest liability.
legal_issues: Test of unfitness under section 8 CDDA 1986
Dishonesty and fiduciary breach in grossing up premiums
Whether Lloyd's findings and Timothy Walker J's judgment created issue estoppel
Whether parallel regulatory proceedings amounted to abuse of process
Appropriate length of disqualification under Sevenoaks Stationers bracket
linked_authorities: Johnson v Gore Wood & Co [2002] 2 AC 1

confidence.notes: Long first-instance judgment with explicit findings, charges, and disqualification period.

enrichment.short_title: Refusal of jury trial in police false imprisonment claim
key_facts: The claimant brought a false imprisonment and malicious prosecution claim after a violent police entry into his girlfriend's flat in 1996.
Section 69 Supreme Court Act 1981 engaged the presumption of jury trial because malicious prosecution and false imprisonment were alleged.
Master Eyre and Judge Chapman refused jury trial on the basis that liability and quantum involved prolonged examination of medical records and expert evidence inconvenient for a jury.
The claim involved about 350 pages of medical records, psychiatric and orthopaedic expert disputes, and a complex future loss of earnings claim.
The Court of Appeal dismissed the second appeal, holding the exception in section 69(1) was satisfied for the whole case.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal to the Court of Appeal against refusal of trial by jury in the Queen's Bench Division.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; trial by judge alone upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Where a civil claim within section 69(1) involves extensive medical documentation and conflicting expert evidence that cannot conveniently be examined with a jury, the section 69(1) exception applies to the whole case even if some discrete quantum issues might theoretically be split under section 69(4).
legal_issues: Scope of the section 69(1) exception for prolonged document examination and scientific investigation
Whether liability and quantum could be split between jury and judge
Meaning of 'conveniently' in section 69(1)
Claimant's constitutional entitlement to jury trial in qualifying claims
index_terms: Darragh v Chief Constable of Thames Valley Police
linked_authorities: Darragh v The Chief Constable of Thames Valley Police (unreported, 16 October 1998)

confidence.notes: Clear procedural ruling with detailed analysis of section 69 and convenience.

enrichment.short_title: Brussels Convention stay over Greek loan dispute

statutes_considered.title: Brussels Convention on Jurisdiction and the Enforcement of Judgments in Civil and Commercial Matters 1968

key_facts: Tavoulareas claimed about US$794,000 outstanding under a London loan agreement connected to a Lloyd's Open Form salvage operation for the Atlas Pride.
The Tsavliris defendants issued Greek proceedings in Piraeus on 8 November 2001 seeking a declaration of non-liability before English service completed.
The defendants argued the Greek court was first seised under Article 21 because service on the Greek Public Prosecutor sufficed under Greek law for a defendant domiciled abroad.
The claimant said service at an outdated London address was a tactical abuse and that Regulation 1348/2000 governed validity of cross-border service.
Tomlinson J stayed the English action and set aside default judgment, declining jurisdiction only for the time being.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory applications to contest jurisdiction and set aside default judgment in a commercial debt claim.
enrichment.outcome: English proceedings stayed; default judgment set aside; jurisdiction not finally declined pending Greek proceedings.
enrichment.ratio: Whether a foreign court was first seised for Article 21 purposes depends on that state's own rules for when proceedings become definitively pending; service on the Greek Public Prosecutor under Article 134 Greek CCP may suffice even where cross-border service on the defendant was defective, and that question is not answered by English service conventions alone.
legal_issues: Identity of causes of action and parties for Article 21
When the Greek court became first seised
Effect of service on the Public Prosecutor under Greek law
Relevance of Regulation 1348/2000 and Phillips v Symes
Whether default judgment should be set aside
linked_authorities: Molins plc v GD SpA [2000] 1 WLR 1741

confidence.notes: Complex foreign-law evidence on an interlocutory ruling; core Article 21 conclusion is clear.

enrichment.short_title: Psychiatric injury after daughter killed by dangerous driving
key_facts: The appellant's 16-year-old daughter Livia was killed when the respondent's car mounted the pavement in January 1998.
The appellant arrived at the cordoned scene, was told of the death by police, and later saw her daughter's body at the mortuary the same evening.
The county court recorder held psychiatric illness was caused only by being told of the death, not by what she saw, and that the mortuary visit was not part of the immediate aftermath.
Psychiatric evidence indicated the scene and mortuary experiences materially contributed to her disorder, not bereavement alone.
The Court of Appeal held the immediate aftermath ran from the accident until she left the mortuary and allowed the appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from dismissal of a secondary-victim psychiatric injury claim in the county court.
enrichment.ratio: For secondary-victim nervous shock claims, the immediate aftermath may comprise a seamless sequence including a prompt mortuary visit to confirm death where that perception materially contributed to psychiatric injury; shock caused by direct perception of the event or aftermath is recoverable even though news of death formed part of that sequence.
legal_issues: Scope of the immediate aftermath after McLoughlin v O'Brian
Whether a mortuary identification visit falls within the aftermath
Whether psychiatric injury was caused by shock through perception rather than mere communication of death
Application of Alcock control mechanisms
linked_authorities: Alcock v Chief Constable of South Yorkshire Police [1992] 1 AC 310
Frost v Chief Constable of South Yorkshire [1999] 2 AC 455
North Glamorgan NHS Trust v Walters [2002] EWCA Civ 1792

confidence.notes: Detailed appellate analysis of nervous-shock control mechanisms with clear outcome.

enrichment.short_title: Section 72 certificate over Dublin removal to Germany
key_facts: A Turkish Kurdish asylum seeker and her four children faced removal from the United Kingdom to Germany under the Dublin Convention.
Germany had accepted responsibility after the family entered the UK clandestinely in 1999 and the husband was removed in March 2002.
The Secretary of State certified the Article 8 claim as manifestly unfounded under section 72(2)(a), permitting removal despite a pending appeal.
Medical evidence showed distress and possible depression in children Newroz and Dilovan, mainly linked to fear of removal and detention.
Hooper J held it was not arguable that removal would substantially affect Article 8 rights or that any interference was outside the range of reasonable responses.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review, with permission granted by the Court of Appeal, of continued maintenance of a section 72 manifestly unfounded certificate.
enrichment.outcome: Application for judicial review refused; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: On judicial review of a section 72 certificate the court asks whether it is arguable an adjudicator would allow an Article 8 appeal; absent evidence of serious and non-speculative mental-health harm from removal, and where Germany will determine the family's future, distress caused by immigration enforcement does not make an Article 8 claim arguable.
legal_issues: Test for reviewing a section 72 manifestly unfounded certificate
Whether removal to Germany would interfere with Article 8(1) rights of the children
Whether any interference was justified under Article 8(2)
Role of adjudicator on proportionality review versus rationality review
linked_authorities: R (Ismet Ali) v SSHD [2003] EWHC 521 Admin

confidence.notes: Long procedural history but clear legal test and refusal outcome on agreed facts.

enrichment.short_title: Terrorism Act membership offence burden of proof
key_facts: Following an Attorney General reference, the court answered questions arising from an acquittal on Terrorism Act 2000 membership counts relating to Hamas-Izz al-Din al-Qassam Brigades.
The defendant had admitted past Hamas membership and training but claimed he left before proscription and had not participated after proscription.
Prosecution counsel at trial conceded only an evidential burden under section 11(2), leading the judge to enter not guilty verdicts.
Section 11(1) criminalises belonging to or professing to belong to a proscribed organisation; section 11(2) provides a limited defence.
The Court of Appeal held section 11(2) imposes a legal burden compatible with Article 6(2) and Article 10.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 Criminal Justice Act 1972 after acquittal at Crown Court.
enrichment.outcome: Reference answered: offence complete under section 11(1) on proof of membership or professed membership; section 11(2) imposes a legal burden compatible with the Convention.
enrichment.ratio: Membership or professed membership of a proscribed organisation is the complete offence under section 11(1), and section 11(2) is a narrow exception imposing a legal burden on the accused that does not derogate from the presumption of innocence and is proportionate in the context of counter-terrorism.
legal_issues: Ingredients of an offence under section 11(1) Terrorism Act 2000
Whether section 11(2) imposes a legal or evidential burden
Compatibility with Article 6(2) after R v Lambert
Compatibility with Article 10 in relation to professing membership
linked_authorities: R v Drummond [2001] 2 Cr App R 25

confidence.notes: Authoritative Attorney General reference with explicit answers to both referred questions.

enrichment.short_title: IAT leave to appeal and Rule 18(6) grounds
key_facts: Two unrelated asylum judicial review claims challenged Immigration Appeal Tribunal refusals of leave to appeal from adjudicators.
Naing, a Burmese NLD supporter, failed on credibility as to a near-arrest in August 2000; Eyaz, a Turkish national, failed on risk on return despite accepted ill-treatment in 1996.
Both claimants sought to rely on grounds not included in their Rule 18 leave applications, or lodged late in Eyaz's case.
Rule 18(6) provides the Tribunal is not required to consider grounds other than those in the application.
Davis J held the Robinson 'obvious point' obligation survives Rule 18(6), but neither case met the high threshold for grounds not raised.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Two consolidated judicial review claims against IAT leave-to-appeal refusals, with an alternative challenge to the vires of Rule 18(6).
enrichment.outcome: Both applications refused; Rule 18(6) held intra vires.
enrichment.ratio: Rule 18(6) does not require the IAT to consider grounds omitted from a leave application, but the Tribunal must still grant leave if an obvious Convention point with strong prospects of success is readily discernible from the papers; that Robinson obligation does not extend to late or undeveloped grounds requiring a fresh merits review.
legal_issues: Effect of Rule 18(6) on grounds not raised in leave applications
Whether Rule 18(6) is ultra vires or requires reading down under section 3 HRA
Application of Robinson v SSHD to IAT leave decisions
When late further grounds must be entertained

confidence.notes: Substantial procedural judgment resolving a common Rule 18 point across two factually distinct claims.

enrichment.short_title: Green Belt enabling development at listed Valley Farm
key_facts: Jewson Holdings appealed under section 78 against refusal of planning permission for four new office buildings and demolition of barns at Valley Farm, Farmoor, Oxfordshire.
The site is in the Green Belt and includes grade II listed buildings.
The claimant argued enabling development under English Heritage guidance was needed to fund repair and long-term conservation of the listed barns.
The inspector found no market testing of the site, insufficient exploration of low-key alternative uses, and failure to show minimum necessary development.
Davis J dismissed the section 288 challenge, holding the inspector's reasoning on enabling development and reasons was lawful.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory challenge under section 288 Town and Country Planning Act 1990 to an inspector's decision dismissing a planning appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; claimant ordered to pay the Secretary of State's costs summarily assessed at £4,663.50.
enrichment.ratio: Enabling development in the Green Belt requires satisfaction of all English Heritage PSPGA criteria, including market testing and demonstration that proposed development is the minimum necessary to bridge a conservation deficit; failure on those threshold criteria lawfully disposes of the appeal without detailed financial appraisal.
legal_issues: Whether the inspector failed to treat English Heritage PSPGA as a material consideration
Whether reasons on minimum necessary enabling development were adequate
Requirement for market testing before enabling development
Very special circumstances to justify inappropriate Green Belt development
linked_authorities: Ashbridge Investments Ltd v Ministry of Housing [1965] 1 WLR 1320
Bolton Metropolitan District Council v Secretary of State [1996] 71 P&CR 309
Granada Hospitality Ltd v Secretary of State [2001] 81 P&CR 505
Save Britain's Heritage v Secretary of State [1991] 2 All ER 10

confidence.notes: Focused planning challenge with clear inspector reasoning and dismissal on multiple independent grounds.
